finding.claim: delete_file calls the boolean is_allowed (imported under the alias require_allowed) and discards the result, so the authorization check never aborts. Any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP DELETE /files/<fid>. The attacker controls fid and needs no grant.
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] at views.py:19, the protected delete operation

trace.note: from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed. The name implies enforcement, but the function only returns a bool.
is_allowed returns True or False and never calls abort.
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') has its return value ignored, so execution continues on a denial.

finding.guards_checked: Checked acl.ensure_allowed, which does abort(403), but delete_file does not call it. Checked for other middleware or decorators: the only before_request hook just sets g.user and does not enforce anything. Rename_file correctly uses ensure_allowed, which shows delete_file is the unguarded outlier.

verdict.guard_found: acl.ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 but is not called by delete_file. The only hook is before_request load_user (views.py:10-12), which copies a client-supplied header into g.user and enforces nothing.
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the boolean is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) as require_allowed, views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement and discards the result, and views.py:19 runs `del STORE[fid]` regardless, so any anonymous DELETE succeeds, unlike rename_file, which calls ensure_allowed at views.py:26.

finding.claim: The user identity is read straight from a client-supplied request header, X-Session-User-Verified, with no authentication or signature check. Any caller can impersonate any user, including a grant holder, and so bypass the ACL on the endpoints that do enforce it.
finding.source: Attacker-set HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, with any value
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') at views.py:26, then the rename at views.py:27. The delete check at views.py:18 is also affected.

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified'), taken as the identity with no validation.
g.user is passed into the ACL check for rename.
The grants lookup is keyed by the attacker-chosen username, so a spoofed owner name passes.

finding.guards_checked: No session, token or signature verification in the repo. No reverse-proxy configuration was present to show the header is stripped or set upstream. The name 'Verified' suggests an upstream proxy sets it, but nothing here enforces that clients cannot supply it. Severity therefore depends on deployment. If the app is directly reachable, this is exploitable. Resource grant names are guessable, for example the file owner's username.

verdict.guard_found: none for identity: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 but only compares the spoofable g.user to grants. Nothing in the repo strips or verifies the header. The delete check at views.py:18 calls is_allowed (aliased as require_allowed) and discards the bool, so that check is a no-op.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the client header, and the rename check at views.py:26 and acl.py:5 trusts that value, so an anonymous caller who sends a grant holder's name passes the ACL at views.py:27; the finding assumes no upstream proxy overwrites the header, and none appears in the repo. The delete check at views.py:18 is worse than the finding says, because it discards the bool.
